result.question: Deep research for SIH 2026 problem SIH26173 (ISRO, Software / Smart Automation): "iTantra - Indian Multilingual TTS & STT Aided Neural Transceiver Radio Access for low bitrate links" — an offline Android app with lightweight STT+TTS for 10 Indian languages (Hindi, Gujarati, Marathi, Kannada, Malayalam, Tamil, Telugu, Odia, Bengali, English) that streams recognized text over WiFi/Bluetooth between two phones acting as a push-to-talk walkie-talkie, judged on accuracy (40%), efficiency (20%), latency (20%), with open-source-only, TinyML-framework, fully-offline restrictions.
result.summary: Split the problem along its five engineering layers — on-device Indic STT models, on-device Indic TTS models, the offline phone-to-phone/embedded transport with text compression, the ISRO low-bitrate satellite/disaster-messaging context that motivates text-over-voice, and the prior-art/competition landscape — so each query targets primary sources (GitHub, HuggingFace, arXiv, Android docs, ISRO pages) with concrete numbers on size, WER, RTF, throughput, and licenses.

angles.query: AI4Bharat IndicConformer IndicWav2Vec sherpa-onnx zipformer Vosk whisper.cpp on-device streaming ASR Indian languages WER Kathbath IndicSUPERB Vistaar model size int8 quantized Android license
angles.rationale: The 40% accuracy weight plus efficiency/latency scoring hinges on picking the right open-license STT model per language; need concrete WER on Indic benchmarks, MB sizes, streaming support, and mobile runtime paths (ONNX Runtime Mobile, TFLite, sherpa-onnx Android API).

angles.rationale: TTS legibility/flow is scored and MMS-TTS's CC-BY-NC license may violate the open-source restriction; need per-language voice availability, model sizes, ARM CPU RTF, sample rates, and Android integration options for each candidate.

angles.query: Android Wi-Fi Direct vs Bluetooth RFCOMM SPP BLE GATT MTU throughput peer-to-peer offline text messaging open source Nearby alternative ESP32 serial bridge Unishox2 Unicode Devanagari short string compression ratio
angles.rationale: The walkie-talkie link and embedded-device bridge need real measured throughput, pairing UX constraints, and API details; Unishox2-style compression of Indic UTF-8 (3 bytes/char) is the lever that makes text fit low-bitrate links and differentiates the design.

angles.rationale: A winning pitch must tie the app to ISRO's actual use case — NavIC/GAGAN one-way messaging and fishermen distress alerts with tiny byte budgets — explaining why transmitting text at <500 bps beats neural voice codecs like Lyra/EnCodec.

angles.query: offline mesh walkie-talkie app Briar Bridgefy Meshtastic architecture Bhashini AI4Bharat on-device deployment Smart India Hackathon winning offline speech recognition Indic code-mixing text normalization TTS
angles.rationale: Knowing existing offline-mesh apps and past SIH/AI4Bharat deployments reveals what judges have seen before and which gaps — code-mixing, number/date normalization, alert priority QoS, store-and-forward relay — a non-generic solution can exploit.

results.title: Unishox2: Guaranteed compression for Unicode short strings (siara-cc)
results.snippet: The exact compression lever named in the research angle: hybrid entropy/dictionary/delta encoder built for short Unicode strings (works even on Arduino/embedded), with delta coding that exploits small codepoint differences within one script — directly applicable to shrinking 3-byte-per-char UTF-8 Devanagari/Dravidian text to fit low-bitrate links. Repo includes a 159-string multilingual test suite and C/JS/Python ports; README/paper give per-language ratios to cite. Primary source, MIT-style open license.

results.title: A Practical Guide to BLE Throughput (Memfault Interrupt)
results.snippet: Concrete measured numbers the transport design needs: default ATT MTU of 23 bytes vs negotiated MTU, BT 4.2 DLE 251-byte payloads, ~784 kbps theoretical GATT throughput and the connection-interval math behind real-world figures — exactly the 'real measured throughput' evidence for choosing BLE vs RFCOMM vs Wi-Fi Direct for the walkie-talkie text link.

results.title: Wi-Fi Direct (P2P) overview — Android Developers
results.snippet: Primary Android documentation for the required WiFi transport mode: WifiP2pManager discovery/connection APIs, no-internet operation over standard Java sockets, group-owner role management and permission requirements — the API-level and pairing-UX constraints (group owner negotiation, location permission) that shape the phone-to-phone PTT design.

results.title: Wi-Fi Aware overview — Android Developers
results.snippet: Official docs for the Android 8.0+ alternative to Wi-Fi Direct: publish/subscribe discovery and direct data paths with no AP, internet, or GO-negotiation friction — a differentiating open transport option (and open-source answer to closed Google Nearby) worth benchmarking against Wi-Fi Direct and Bluetooth in the solution.

results.title: Meshtastic — Initial Configuration (phone ↔ ESP32/LoRa node)
results.snippet: Working prior art for the embedded-device bridge requirement: open-source LoRa mesh firmware on ESP32/nRF52 nodes that Android apps join over BLE or USB serial, with tiny text-message payload budgets — a proven pattern (and competition landscape reference) for streaming STT text to an off-grid radio node.

results.title: ESP32 Bluetooth Classic (SPP) with Arduino IDE — Random Nerd Tutorials
results.snippet: Practical implementation reference for the ESP32-as-embedded-endpoint path: BluetoothSerial creates a transparent Serial↔Bluetooth-SPP bridge, letting an Android phone stream recognized text to an ESP32 over RFCOMM exactly as the problem statement's 'embedded device' mode requires.

results.title: ai4bharat/indic-conformer-600m-multilingual - Hugging Face model card
results.snippet: Primary source for the strongest open Indic STT model: multilingual Conformer (~600M params) covering all 22 scheduled languages incl. the 10 required, with hybrid CTC + RNNT decoding modes and per-language benchmark WERs. Key basis for accuracy (40% criterion) claims; smaller per-language IndicConformer variants also exist for on-device use.

results.title: sherpa-onnx Discussion #3199: ASR pretrained models for Hindi, Tamil and other Indic languages
results.snippet: Directly answers the mobile-runtime question: community has converted AI4Bharat IndicConformer to sherpa-onnx NeMo-CTC format (Malayalam done as proof), making offline CPU-only Indic ASR runnable via the sherpa-onnx Android API — the concrete IndicConformer-to-Android deployment path for the app.

results.title: Vistaar: Diverse Benchmarks and Training Sets for Indian Language ASR (Interspeech 2023)
results.snippet: The benchmark ground truth for the accuracy criterion: 59 test sets (Kathbath, FLEURS, CommonVoice, IndicTTS, MUCS, GramVaani) across 12 Indian languages; IndicWhisper achieves lowest WER on 39/59 benchmarks (avg -4.1 WER vs baselines). Use these tables to justify per-language model choice with concrete WER numbers.

results.title: Vosk Models list (Alpha Cephei) - sizes and licenses per language
results.snippet: Apache-2.0, ~50 MB streaming small models with zero-latency streaming API and Android bindings; lists concrete model sizes for Hindi, Telugu, Tamil, Gujarati and Indian English. The lightweight/efficiency baseline (20% efficiency + 20% latency criteria), but Indic coverage is incomplete (no Odia/Marathi etc.), exposing a gap a hybrid design must fill.

results.title: sherpa-onnx: Zipformer-transducer streaming models (int8) documentation
results.snippet: Concrete numbers for streaming ASR on Android: Zipformer2 transducer models with int8 dynamic quantization cutting size ~50% (e.g. encoder ~315MB fp32 vs int8 variants; small models tens of MB), ready-made ARM64 APKs — the reference architecture for low-latency pause-detected streaming STT required by the walkie-talkie mode.

results.title: AI4Bharat/IndicWav2Vec - pretraining/fine-tuning/eval for Indic wav2vec2
results.snippet: 317M-param wav2vec2-large models pretrained on 40 Indian languages, fine-tuned per language on Kathbath with published WERs; MIT-style open release. Relevant as an accuracy alternative, but its size and non-streaming CTC decoding make it a comparison point rather than the on-device pick.

results.title: Bluetooth Chat Apps Compared: BitChat, Bridgefy, Briar & More
results.snippet: Direct prior-art comparison of the offline mesh messaging apps judges will know (Briar via Bluetooth/Wi-Fi Direct, Bridgefy via BLE mesh, BitChat), including transport choices, encryption, range (~100m direct, 500m+ multi-hop) and battery drain (18-28% over 8h) — none do speech/STT/TTS, which is exactly the differentiation gap iTantra can exploit.

results.title: Store & Forward Module Settings | Meshtastic (official docs)
results.snippet: Primary source on how Meshtastic implements store-and-forward relay over LoRa (ESP32+PSRAM server nodes resending message history to clients that left range) — the concrete reference architecture for a store-and-forward/message-priority QoS feature and for an ESP32/LoRa embedded bridge that would make an SIH26173 solution non-generic.

results.title: Normalization of code-switched text for speech synthesis (Interspeech 2022)
results.snippet: Peer-reviewed paper on exactly the code-mixing gap: code-mixed Indic text breaks TTS via language identification, spelling normalization and pronunciation modeling failures — evidence and methods for a Hinglish/code-switch handling layer most hackathon teams will omit.

results.title: Indic Text Normalization — Kenpath (open-source WFST library)
results.snippet: Open-source WFST-based library converting numbers, dates, currency and measurements into spoken form for Indic TTS/ASR (e.g. '25 ko' must be read 'pachchees' not 'twenty-five') — a ready, license-compatible building block for the number/date normalization differentiator flagged in the research goal.

results.title: Smart India Hackathon SIH 2026 Problem Statements (CSV/JSON/MD)
results.snippet: Community catalogue confirming SIH26173 'iTantra' (ISRO, Software, Smart Automation/Space Tech); searches show no public GitHub solutions for it yet — the competition field is greenfield, so differentiation must come from execution (code-mixing, alert QoS, mesh relay) rather than beating an established reference repo.

results.title: AI4Bharat — Automatic Speech Recognition (IndicWav2Vec, IndicWhisper, IndicConformer)
results.snippet: Primary landscape source on the Indic ASR models past teams and judges have seen deployed (IndicConformer covering all 22 scheduled languages, TFLite/MediaPipe on-device paths, models open-sourced via Bhashini) — the baseline any SIH26173 entry will use, defining where a team must go beyond stock AI4Bharat checkpoints to stand out.

results.title: NavIC and MSS based Messaging and Surveillance Applications (ISRO, ICG-14)
results.snippet: Primary ISRO presentation giving the hard byte budget: NavIC broadcast messages carry ~220 user-definable bits per message, with Message IDs 20/21 allocated to INCOIS for PFZ, high-wave, cyclone and tsunami alerts. This is the ground truth for why iTantra must ship compressed TEXT, not audio — a whole sentence must fit in tens of bytes.

results.title: NavIC Messaging Service – An Update (ISRO, ICG-16, 2022)
results.snippet: Official ISRO update on the NavIC short-message service used by INCOIS to broadcast fishing-zone, cyclone and tsunami alerts to fishermen beyond terrestrial coverage — the exact one-way, low-bitrate alert-dissemination pipeline that an offline TTS 'announce alert at max volume' feature plugs into.

results.title: Distress Alert Transmitter (DAT / DAT-SG) for Fishermen
results.snippet: Describes ISRO's second-generation Distress Alert Transmitter: satellite alerts routed via INMCC to Coast Guard, with DAT-SG connecting to mobile phones over Bluetooth so messages are read in native languages via an app — almost a verbatim description of iTantra's embedded-device-over-Bluetooth + multilingual TTS requirement.

results.title: GEMINI Device (GAGAN Enabled Mariner's Instrument for Navigation & Information)
results.snippet: GEMINI is the GAGAN-based receiver + phone-app system delivering cyclone/tsunami/PFZ warnings to fishermen up to 300 nautical miles offshore, where phones lose coverage at 10-12 km — the real-world last-mile scenario that motivates announcing received text as non-interruptible spoken alerts in the fisherman's language.

results.title: Nabhmitra: Satellite-Based Two-Way Safety Device for Fishermen (ISRO SAC)
results.snippet: ISRO Space Applications Centre's Nabhmitra adds two-way satellite messaging with an emergency button and boat location — evidence that ISRO's roadmap is short two-way text over satellite, i.e., the uplink side (fisherman speaks, STT sends compact text) of the iTantra pitch.

results.title: Ultra-Low-Bitrate Speech Coding with Pretrained Transformers (arXiv)
results.snippet: Baseline for the codec comparison: even state-of-the-art neural speech codecs (Lyra ~3.2 kbps, EnCodec 1.5 kbps, research systems ~600 bps) sit well above a 220-bit NavIC message budget, while text of a spoken sentence is ~100-300 bits after compression — the quantitative case for text-transport (STT→text→TTS) over neural voice codecs on ISRO links.

results.title: AI4Bharat/Indic-TTS (GitHub) — FastPitch + HiFi-GAN TTS for 13 Indian languages, MIT-licensed
results.snippet: The strongest license-safe Indic TTS base: MIT-licensed FastPitch + HiFi-GAN V1 models covering all 10 required languages (Hindi, Bengali, Gujarati, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Odia, Tamil, Telugu + English via related work), trained jointly on male/female speakers and shown best-performing in AI4Bharat's evaluation. Exportable to ONNX for sherpa-onnx/ONNX Runtime Mobile Android deployment — directly satisfies the 'open-source only, offline' restriction where MMS-TTS cannot.

results.title: facebook/mms-tts (Hugging Face) — Meta MMS VITS TTS collection, CC-BY-NC 4.0
results.snippet: Confirms the licensing landmine the research angle flags: the MMS-TTS VITS models (1100+ languages, per-language checkpoints incl. mms-tts-hin/tam/tel/ben/ory/mal, ~16 kHz output, generator-only inference checkpoints) are CC-BY-NC 4.0 — non-commercial and arguably outside SIH's 'open-source only' bar, so they should be treated as a fallback/baseline only, not the headline solution.

results.title: sherpa-onnx VITS pretrained TTS models — official k2-fsa docs
results.snippet: Primary Android integration path: sherpa-onnx runs VITS/Piper/MMS ONNX models fully offline on Android with a Kotlin API, lists downloadable per-language voices with concrete sizes (e.g. int8-quantized VITS ~37 MB vs 116 MB fp32) — the practical runtime for shipping AI4Bharat or Piper voices in the iTantra app and for measuring the RTF/model-size metrics scored under Efficiency and Latency.

results.title: rhasspy/piper-voices (Hugging Face) — Piper voice catalog, MIT, 35 languages
results.snippet: Authoritative catalog for checking Piper's per-language Indic coverage (MIT-licensed, low/medium/high tiers roughly 20-30/60-80/100+ MB); Indic coverage is sparse (no official voices for most of the 10 required languages), which is exactly the gap analysis needed — Piper's fast single-pass VITS runs real-time on phone CPUs but the team must train/convert Indic voices rather than download them.

results.title: ai4bharat/IndicF5 (Hugging Face) — near-human polyglot TTS for 11 Indian languages
results.snippet: IndicF5 covers 11 Indian languages (incl. Bengali, Gujarati, Hindi, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Odia, Tamil, Telugu) with near-human quality from 1,417 h of speech — useful as the quality ceiling reference, but it's a heavy flow-matching model unsuited to low/mid-range phones, so the writeup should position it as why the solution chose lighter FastPitch/VITS models instead.

results.title: espeak-ng (GitHub) — GPLv3 formant synthesizer, 100+ languages incl. all 10 target languages
results.snippet: The guaranteed-coverage fallback and phonemizer: tiny formant-synthesis engine (all 100+ voices in a few MB, negligible RTF/RAM) supporting Hindi, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, and the other target languages on Android under GPLv3 — also the grapheme-to-phoneme front end Piper depends on, so it matters both as a legibility floor and as an integration dependency.

claims.claim: The Meshtastic Android app can connect to a LoRa mesh node (e.g., an ESP32-based device) over USB Serial or Bluetooth, confirming that a phone-to-embedded-radio bridge over Bluetooth or USB serial is an already-proven, open-source deployment pattern directly reusable for the SIH26173 'stream text to an embedded device' requirement.
claims.quote: Open the app, connect to the device from your phone over USB Serial or Bluetooth. Once paired and connected...

claims.claim: Meshtastic supports three phone/client-to-node connection transports — Bluetooth (Android App, Web Client), Serial/USB (Python CLI, Web Client, Android App), and Network WiFi/TCP — with the WiFi/TCP network connection limited to ESP32 devices only.
claims.quote: Network (WiFi/TCP): Limited to ESP32 devices; supports Web Client, Android App, iOS App, and Python CLI

claims.claim: Sub-GHz LoRa deployments in EU-style regulatory bands operate under a 10% hourly duty-cycle cap (e.g., EU 868 at 869.4-869.65 MHz, 27 dBm), a concrete regulatory constraint illustrating why bytes-per-message budgets matter on low-bitrate LoRa links of the kind an iTantra ESP32/LoRa bridge would use (India's 865-867 MHz ISM band is similarly constrained).
claims.quote: EU_433 and EU_868 have to adhere to an hourly duty cycle limitation of 10%

claims.claim: Meshtastic clients exist across Android, iOS/iPadOS, macOS, Web, and Python CLI, indicating a mature multi-platform open-source offline-mesh ecosystem that constitutes prior art / competition landscape for any SIH walkie-talkie-over-LoRa extension.
claims.quote: Android App (all connection types); iOS/iPadOS App (network and Bluetooth); macOS App (network connections); Web Client (all connection types); Python CLI (serial and network)

claims.claim: The Meshtastic initial-configuration page documents regional frequency allocations (e.g., US 902.0-928.0 MHz at 30 dBm, 100% duty cycle) but does NOT document message size limits or link bitrates, so those numbers must be sourced from other Meshtastic/LoRa documentation rather than this page.
claims.quote: Message limits and bitrates are not documented on this page.

claims.claim: Android's Wi-Fi Direct (P2P) APIs let two phones connect and exchange data directly over Wi-Fi with no access point or internet, satisfying the SIH26173 requirement for fully offline phone-to-phone text streaming.
claims.quote: Wi-Fi Direct (P2P) allows devices with the appropriate hardware to connect directly to each other via Wi-Fi without an intermediate access point.

claims.claim: Wi-Fi Direct offers faster throughput and longer range than Bluetooth, making it the higher-bandwidth of the two offline transports the problem statement allows (WiFi/Bluetooth).
claims.quote: communicate over a speedy connection across distances much longer than a Bluetooth connection

claims.claim: On Android 13+ (API 33), discoverPeers() and connect() require the runtime NEARBY_WIFI_DEVICES permission, while apps targeting earlier Android versions need ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION instead — a real UX/permissions constraint for a walkie-talkie app on low/mid-range phones.
claims.quote: On apps that target Android 13 (API level 33) and higher, both `discoverPeers()` and `connect()` require the `android.permission.NEARBY_WIFI_DEVICES` permission. On apps that target earlier versions of Android, these methods require the `ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION` permission instead.

claims.claim: Wi-Fi P2P is supported from API level 14 (Android 4.0), so essentially every low/mid-range Android phone in India can run it, and data transfer is done over ordinary TCP sockets (server on the group owner, e.g. port 8888) rather than any proprietary protocol.
claims.quote: <uses-sdk android:minSdkVersion="14" />

claims.claim: Peer discovery uses a group-owner model: one device hosts the P2P group (createGroup) and the other joins, and discovery operations (discoverPeers, discoverServices, requestPeers) require the device's Location Mode to be enabled — a practical failure mode to handle in the field.
claims.quote: Creates a peer-to-peer group with the current device as the group owner

claims.claim: Wi-Fi Aware lets Android devices running Android 8.0 (API level 26) or higher discover and connect directly to each other with no access point, internet, or any other connectivity — a fully offline peer-to-peer transport suitable for the SIH26173 phone-to-phone text link.
claims.quote: Wi-Fi Aware capabilities enable devices running Android 8.0 (API level 26) and higher to discover and connect directly to each other without any other type of connectivity between them.

claims.claim: Wi-Fi Aware's connectionless sendMessage() path is limited to roughly 255 bytes per message and offers no delivery, ordering, or de-duplication guarantees — so transcribed sentences either need compression to fit this budget plus an app-level ack scheme, or a socket-based data path instead.
claims.quote: Messages are generally used for lightweight messaging, as they might not be delivered (or be delivered out-of-order or more than once) and are limited to about 255 bytes in length.

claims.claim: Beyond short messages, Wi-Fi Aware supports full bidirectional client-server networking between two devices using standard TCP sockets (ServerSocket/Socket over IPv6), which provides a reliable stream channel for continuous STT-text transfer.
claims.quote: Wi-Fi Aware supports client-server networking between two Wi-Fi Aware devices.

claims.claim: Wi-Fi Aware network connections deliver higher throughput over longer range than Bluetooth connections, which is the documented basis for preferring it over BT Classic/BLE when both phones support it.
claims.quote: Wi-Fi Aware network connections support higher throughput rates across longer distances than Bluetooth connections.

claims.claim: Wi-Fi Aware is optional hardware (apps must check PackageManager.FEATURE_WIFI_AWARE) and can become unavailable at runtime when the user disables Wi-Fi or Location — a practical risk on the low/mid-range phones targeted by SIH26173, so a fallback transport (Wi-Fi Direct or Bluetooth) is needed.
claims.quote: Wi-Fi Aware may exist on the device, but may not be currently available because the user has disabled Wi-Fi or Location.

claims.claim: The default BLE ATT MTU is only 23 bytes (fitting one Link Layer packet), while the spec allows negotiating up to a 512-byte ATT payload — so an un-negotiated GATT link carries at most ~20 usable bytes per write/notification after the 3-byte ATT header, which is why short-string compression of Indic Unicode text matters per-packet.
claims.quote: 23 bytes (which allows the packet to fit in one LL packet) ... 3 bytes of ATT packet overhead

claims.claim: Theoretical BLE application throughput ranges from ~0.226 Mbps (BLE 4.0, 1M PHY, default 23-byte MTU) through ~0.803 Mbps (BLE 4.2 with 251-byte Data Length Extension) to ~1.434 Mbps (BLE 5.0, 2M PHY + DLE) — all vastly exceeding the bytes-per-second needed to stream sentence text, validating text-over-BLE as a transport for the walkie-talkie app.
claims.quote: With 251-byte payload: "~0.803 Mbps" ... BLE 5.0 (2M PHY + Data Length Extension): With 251-byte payload: "~1.434 Mbps"

claims.claim: Real-world phone throughput is far below theoretical: most iOS devices support a 185-byte MTU, 7 packets per connection interval, and a 15 ms minimum connection interval, yielding about 12.2 kBytes/sec (~0.10 Mbps) achievable GATT throughput — a realistic planning number for phone-to-phone or phone-to-ESP32 BLE links.
claims.quote: Most iOS devices support a 185 byte MTU and 7 packets per connection interval

claims.claim: The BLE connection interval is bounded between 7.5 ms and 4 s, and a device limited to one packet per connection event achieves only ~0.029 Mbps even at the fastest 7.5 ms interval — connection-parameter negotiation, not radio bitrate, dominates worst-case latency and throughput for short text messages.
claims.quote: Some older devices only support one packet per connection interval

claims.claim: Per-exchange protocol overhead is concrete and large at small payloads: a BLE 4.0 single-packet exchange takes 708 μs (328 μs data + 150 μs T_IFS + 80 μs ACK + 150 μs T_IFS) to move 27 payload bytes, with 4 bytes L2CAP overhead per packet, capping Link Layer data throughput at ~0.381 Mbps on a 1 Mbps radio.
claims.quote: 328μs data packet + 150μs T_IFS + 80μs ACK + 150μs T_IFS = 708μs

claims.claim: ESP32 Bluetooth Classic serial (SPP-style) communication can be implemented in the Arduino IDE using the BluetoothSerial library, with the device advertised under a chosen name via SerialBT.begin(), making the ESP32 usable as a wireless serial bridge for text data from a phone.
claims.quote: SerialBT.begin("ESP32test"); //Bluetooth device name

claims.claim: An Android phone can pair with the ESP32 over Bluetooth Classic and exchange text bidirectionally using the free 'Serial Bluetooth Terminal' app from the Google Play Store, with standard serial-style read/write calls (SerialBT.write, SerialBT.read, SerialBT.available) on the ESP32 side — demonstrating a working phone-to-embedded-device text channel of the kind SIH26173 requires for streaming STT output to an embedded device.
claims.quote: Users pair via the Serial Bluetooth Terminal Android app (available on Google Play Store). The device appears in the app's pairing list after enabling phone Bluetooth.

claims.claim: This ESP32 Bluetooth Classic approach works only with Android smartphones, not iPhones — a real constraint for the transport layer, since iOS lacks general Bluetooth Classic SPP support (an Android-only limitation that is acceptable for SIH26173, which mandates an Android app).
claims.quote: this project is only compatible with Android smartphones.

claims.claim: The demo parses incoming Bluetooth text as newline-delimited messages (accumulating characters until '\n'), i.e. a simple line-based framing protocol suitable for sending sentence-at-a-time text — the same message-framing pattern an STT-to-embedded-device link would use.
claims.quote: if (incomingChar != '\n'){ message += String(incomingChar); }

claims.claim: The tutorial's wired serial monitor link runs at 115200 baud (Serial.begin(115200)), which bounds the demonstrated bridge throughput at roughly 11.5 KB/s on the UART side — far more than needed for compressed sentence text.
claims.quote: Serial.begin(115200)

claims.claim: Unishox2 is a hybrid encoder purpose-built for compressing short Unicode strings individually, combining entropy coding (fixed prefix-free codes per letter), dictionary coding (repeating letter sets), and delta coding for Unicode characters — the exact regime needed for sentence-length Indic text messages, where general-purpose compressors fail.

claims.claim: Unishox2 supports the entire Unicode character set with UTF-8 as input and output encoding, using delta coding for non-Latin code points — meaning Devanagari, Dravidian, Odia and Bengali scripts can be compressed, though the README itself publishes no per-script compression-ratio benchmarks (numbers live in the linked figshare paper, not the repo page).
claims.quote: "Unishox supports the entire Unicode character set. As of now it supports UTF-8 as input and output encoding." ... "For Unicode characters, delta coding is used."

claims.claim: Unishox2 explicitly targets low-bitrate radio links and constrained embedded devices — its stated applications include text transfer over LoRa and BLE and use on Arduino/ESP8266-class hardware — which matches SIH26173's WiFi/Bluetooth-to-embedded-device transport requirement and an ESP32/LoRa bridge design.

claims.claim: IndicWhisper (Whisper-medium fine-tuned per-language by AI4Bharat) achieves the lowest WER on 39 of the 59 Vistaar benchmarks spanning 12 Indian languages, with an average WER reduction of 4.1 points over compared systems — making Vistaar the reference accuracy benchmark suite (Kathbath, Kathbath-Hard, FLEURS, CommonVoice, IndicTTS, MUCS, Gramvaani) for the 9 Indic languages in SIH26173.

claims.claim: On the Hindi subset of Vistaar, IndicWhisper (average WER 13.6, Kathbath 10.3) substantially beats the commercial cloud APIs Google STT (23.9) and Azure STT (20.0) as well as open IndicWav2Vec (21.0) — evidence that open fine-tuned models can exceed proprietary SDKs banned by the SIH26173 rules.

claims.claim: Kenpath's Indic Text Normalization is an open-source WFST-based library built on Pynini that converts numbers, dates, currency, and measurements into spoken form for TTS/ASR pipelines — directly addressing the number/date normalization gap for Indic TTS identified as a differentiation opportunity for SIH26173.

claims.claim: The library covers all 9 Indic languages required by SIH26173 plus English (IN): its 19 supported languages include Hindi, Bengali, Marathi, Telugu, Kannada, Tamil, Malayalam, Gujarati, and Odia is NOT listed — meaning Odia normalization would need custom work in a solution built on this library.
claims.quote: Hindi, Bengali, Marathi, Telugu, Kannada, Tamil, Malayalam, Gujarati, Punjabi, Assamese, Nepali, Sanskrit, Maithili, Bhojpuri, Magahi, Chhattisgarhi, Bodo, Dogri, and English (IN).

claims.claim: The library claims 1-5 ms average normalization latency on CPU with deterministic output, versus ~500 ms for local LLM approaches and ~2000 ms for API-based approaches — making it viable for the low-latency, offline, CPU-only constraints of the SIH26173 problem.
claims.quote: 1 – 5 ms average normalization latency

claims.claim: The library is licensed under Apache 2.0 and hosted on GitHub (github.com/kenpath/indic-text-normalization), satisfying SIH26173's open-source-only restriction, and is positioned as an extension of NVIDIA NeMo's text normalization for Indic languages.
claims.quote: Open source under Apache 2.0.

claims.claim: The library handles 12 semiotic classes (cardinals, ordinals, decimals, fractions, dates, time, phone numbers, measurements, currency, electronic addresses, Roman numerals, abbreviations) and requires no GPU, running as deterministic FST traversal rather than autoregressive generation.
claims.quote: Deterministic FST traversal, not autoregressive token generation.

claims.claim: Conventional TTS text normalization pipelines cannot handle code-switched Indic text (Malayalam-English), and as of 2022 no normalization modules existed for Malayalam-English code-switched social media input — evidence that code-mixing handling is a genuine gap an SIH solution can differentiate on.
claims.quote: To the best of our knowledge, there exist no normalization modules that can handle Malayalam-English code-switched input social media text.

claims.claim: In real Malayalam-English social media text collected from Twitter, Malayalam written in Latin (English) script vastly outnumbers Malayalam in native script (7,580 romanized Malayalam words vs 2,150 native-script words, plus 11,500 English words and 420 intra-word code-switched words), so an Indic TTS front-end must handle romanized input, not just native-script Unicode.
claims.quote: In the data collected from twitter as shown in Table 1, 2150 words are in Malayalam script and 20,000 words in English script.

claims.claim: The paper's two-stage normalization approach (Stage 1: Unicode-range script detection, punctuation/letter-case correction, English dictionary lookup; Stage 2: Finite State Transducer-based Malayalam normalizer for romanized and intra-word code-switched words) achieved 87.5% average word-level accuracy against a manually normalized reference, with per-category accuracy of 85% (English words), 100% (Malayalam words), 81% (Malayalam in English script), 87% (intra-word code-switched), 75% (special characters).
claims.quote: Total average accuracy of 87.5% was obtained.

claims.claim: Text normalization measurably improves code-switched TTS quality: their Tacotron 2-based TTS fed normalized input scored MOS 3.82 (30 listeners, 30 sentences), beating two existing monolingual Malayalam TTS systems (MOS 3.3 and 3.25) given non-normalized transliterated code-switched input.
claims.quote: A mean opinion score of 3.82 was obtained for the TTS output based on our developed text normalization module.

claims.claim: Malayalam's abugida properties (15 vowels, 36 consonants, inherent vowel after each consonant, high agglutination, and no phoneme-set overlap subset relation with English) make phonetic sub-unit splitting with inherent-vowel restoration necessary for normalizing romanized Malayalam — a script-specific complication any 10-language Indic TTS front-end must engineer around.
claims.quote: Malayalam words have high level of agglutination and vowel missing in this make text normalization more challenging.

claims.claim: GEMINI (GAGAN Enabled Mariner's Instrument for Navigation & Information) is a portable satellite receiver developed by INCOIS in collaboration with the Airports Authority of India, using ISRO/AAI's GAGAN satellite system, to push emergency alerts and ocean information to fishermen — a concrete ISRO-ecosystem precedent for the satellite-based, low-bitrate message dissemination context behind SIH26173/iTantra.

result.summary: The verified research establishes that no single open-source model family covers all 10 required languages for on-device STT or TTS, so a winning SIH26173 solution must be a deliberately engineered hybrid: AI4Bharat's MIT-licensed models (IndicConformer-600M, IndicWav2Vec, Indic-TTS FastPitch+HiFiGAN) cover the 9 Indic languages with the best accuracy pedigree but ship no mobile runtime and need custom export/quantization, while the projects that DO ship Android-ready runtimes (Vosk, sherpa-onnx, Piper) have large per-language gaps — Vosk covers only 4-5 of 10 languages (with Telugu at an unusable 87.9 WER), sherpa-onnx's streaming ASR catalog covers only Bengali+English among the targets, and official Piper voices exist for just 6 of 10 languages. Licensing is a scoring trap: Meta MMS-TTS covers all 10 languages but is CC-BY-NC 4.0 (non-commercial, not OSI open source), and even inside the MIT-tagged Piper repo individual Indic voices inherit non-commercial dataset licenses, so eligibility must be audited per-voice. Feasibility of the latency criterion is confirmed: Piper/small-VITS-class TTS runs at RTF 0.35-0.8 single-threaded on a Raspberry Pi 4 (weaker than mid-range phone cores), and streaming transducer ASR at this size class budgets roughly 90 MB per language before int8 quantization. The differentiating build path the evidence supports is: distill/quantize AI4Bharat checkpoints (trained on the open 10,736-hour Vistaar corpus, benchmarked on the 59-benchmark Vistaar suite where open fine-tuned models already beat Google/Azure cloud APIs) into a sherpa-onnx/ONNX-Runtime Android pipeline, filling English with Vosk/Piper — because no off-the-shelf stack does this today.

findings.claim: sherpa-onnx is the best Android deployment runtime but its pretrained streaming-ASR catalog has a massive Indic gap the team must fill themselves: among the 10 target languages, the official streaming Zipformer-transducer catalog covers only Bengali (a repackaged Vosk/Alphacep model) plus English — no Hindi, Gujarati, Marathi, Kannada, Malayalam, Tamil, Telugu, or Odia. The Bengali model's footprint (encoder 87 MB + decoder 2 MB + joiner 1 MB ≈ 90 MB fp32 per language) sets the realistic per-language budget for streaming transducers at this size class; comparable models on the same page show int8 quantization cuts encoders ~3x (250 MB → 68 MB), so int8 is mandatory for a 10-language app.
findings.evidence: Official k2-fsa docs page fetched live: full model list is Bengali, Chinese (6), Korean, English (3), zh-en bilingual — zero hi/ta/te/kn/ml/mr/gu/or models; Bengali page states verbatim 'This model is from https://huggingface.co/alphacep/vosk-model-small-streaming-bn' and lists 'encoder.onnx: 87M, decoder.onnx: 2.0M, joiner.onnx: 1.0M'. Corroborated by k2-fsa/sherpa-onnx Discussion #3199 asking for (absent) Hindi/Tamil Indic models. Merges claims 9, 10 (both 3-0).

findings.claim: AI4Bharat IndicWav2Vec covers 9 of the 10 target languages (fine-tuned ASR for Bengali, Gujarati, Hindi, Marathi, Odia, Tamil, Telugu plus separate Kannada and Malayalam models; English excepted) and is fully MIT-licensed across pretrained, fine-tuned, and language models — but the repo (last updated June 2022) provides NO first-party mobile path: 'Mobile — Coming soon', no ONNX/TorchScript export code, no streaming support, only Flask server deployment. Any Android use requires the team's own export/quantization work — simultaneously a differentiation opportunity and a schedule risk vs sherpa-onnx/Vosk which ship Android runtimes.
findings.evidence: README verified live (commit 8d6f75c): download table lists all 9+2 language models with fairseq/HF links; 'IndicWav2Vec is MIT-licensed... covering all the pretrained, fine-tuned and language models'; Deployment section verbatim 'Mobile - Coming soon', only flask_dep.py documented; the only occurrence of 'stream' in the README is 'downstream'; repo tree contains no android/onnx/export code. Minor notes: HF-ported checkpoints carry an apache-2.0 tag (equally permissive), and the ONNX/TorchScript section is an empty placeholder rather than literally labeled 'Coming soon'. findings.claim: AI4Bharat Indic-TTS is the license-safest full-coverage TTS foundation: monolingual FastPitch acoustic models + HiFi-GAN V1 vocoder, each trained jointly on male and female speakers (two voices per language), for 13 languages including 9 of 10 targets in the README — and crucially the v1-checkpoints-release GitHub release also includes en.zip (Indian English) and en+hi.zip (Hinglish code-mixed), making practical coverage 10/10 SIH languages. The repo has a real MIT LICENSE.txt and states 'We open-source all models' on the Bhashini platform. Caveat: each checkpoint zip is ~1.5 GB of training checkpoints, so mobile deployment requires export/pruning/quantization (or vocoder swap) by the team.
findings.evidence: README verified: 13 languages listed verbatim, 'monolingual models with FastPitch and HiFi-GAN V1, trained jointly on male and female speakers'; architecture backed by ICASSP 2023 paper arXiv:2211.09536 (ablation selected FastPitch+HiFiGAN-V1). GitHub API confirms the release holds 16 checkpoint zips (~1.5 GB each) including en and en+hi, and the /license endpoint detects MIT via LICENSE.txt. The English/Hinglish checkpoints existing despite English's absence from the README language list is the verified surprise that closes the 10th-language TTS gap. Merges claims 14, 15, 16 (2-1, 3-0, 3-0).

findings.claim: Meta MMS-TTS is a coverage-complete but license-risky option: per-language VITS checkpoints (~36M params each) exist for all 10 required languages among its 1107 (hin, ben, tam, tel, kan, mal, mar, guj, ory, eng — ISO 639-3 addressed as facebook/mms-tts-{code}), but every checkpoint is CC-BY-NC 4.0 — a non-commercial license that is not OSI-approved open source (NC clause violates OSD criterion 6). Under SIH26173's 'open-source only, no proprietary/commercial voice SDKs' rule this is at minimum a flag-it-explicitly risk and at worst disqualifying; safer to use MMS-TTS only as a quality baseline or for languages with no MIT alternative, with the constraint disclosed.
findings.evidence: Primary cards fetched live: facebook/mms-tts states 'supports 1107 languages' with license cc-by-nc-4.0; per-language repos confirmed live for the rarest targets (mms-tts-ory Odia VITS 36.3M params, mms-tts-guj, mms-tts-kan); fairseq MMS README confirms CC-BY-NC 4.0 for code and weights, no relicensing found. Merges claims 17, 18 (both 3-0).

findings.claim: On-device TTS latency targets are demonstrably achievable, and sherpa-onnx's hidden Indic TTS inventory partially covers the gap: the official VITS docs page lists 100+ models / 40+ languages but no Indic ones — the GitHub tts-models release assets (642 assets, ~255 distinct VITS models) DO contain Indic voices (Piper Hindi pratham/priyamvada/rohan, Piper Malayalam arjun/meera, Coqui + Mimic3 Bengali, Mimic3 Gujarati). Benchmarks on a Raspberry Pi 4B (ARM Cortex-A72, weaker than mid-range phone big cores, i.e., conservative): vits-icefall-zh-aishell3 RTF 0.365 (1 thread) / 0.156 (4 threads); Piper-class English models RTF 0.79-0.81 (1 thread) / ~0.35 (4 threads) — comfortably faster than real time, directly serving the 20%-weighted latency/RTF criterion. Warning: large unoptimized VITS (vits-ljs RTF 6.06) is 8x too slow, so model class selection is decisive.
findings.evidence: Docs page verified verbatim: 'Since there are more than 100 pre-trained models for over 40 languages, we don't list all of them on this page'; RTF tables confirmed exactly (0.365/0.156 aishell3; 0.812/0.349 glados; 0.790/0.357 libritts_r) on 'Raspberry Pi 4 Model B Rev 1.5'; independent GitHub API enumeration of the tts-models release found the named Indic VITS/Piper/Coqui/Mimic3 assets. Merges claims 19, 20 (both 3-0).

findings.claim: Piper TTS (the natural Android-friendly TTS runtime) officially covers only 6 of the 10 required languages — hi, bn, mr, ml, te, en exist as rhasspy/piper-voices directories; Gujarati, Kannada, Tamil, and Odia have NO official voices and would need custom training (community Tamil voices exist outside the catalog). Licensing is per-voice, not per-repo: the repo is MIT-tagged, but hi_IN-pratham was trained on AI4Bharat corpus data under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (non-commercial) while mr_IN-google uses OpenSLR-64 data under permissive CC BY-SA 4.0 — every voice's MODEL_CARD must be audited for SIH eligibility. Also note the only official Bengali voice is bn_BD (Bangladesh accent), not bn_IN.
findings.evidence: HF tree API verified live: language directories include hi, bn, mr, ml, te, en and lack gu, kn, ta, or ('ka' is Georgian). MODEL_CARDs verified verbatim: hi_IN/pratham dataset license 'creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-sa/4.0' (AI4Bharat indicnlp_corpus, trained by community member PravalX); mr_IN/google dataset openslr.org/64 under 'Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International', 22,050 Hz. A third-party tts.ai page listing Piper Gujarati/Kannada/Tamil voices was investigated and discounted (commercial cloud voice branding, absent from the official repo). Merges claims 21, 22 (both 3-0).

result.caveats: Two claims could not be verified due to infrastructure errors (verifier agents failed, neither confirmed nor refuted): (1) IndicWav2Vec's benchmark WER table (Hindi 16.0/14.7 with LM; Bengali 16.6/13.6; Tamil 27.3/25.0 — implying KenLM decoding buys ~1.3-3 WER points), and (2) the claim that all Indic Piper voices exist only at the 'medium' 22,050 Hz tier at ~63-77 MB per ONNX file (~400 MB for 6 languages) — treat both as plausible but unconfirmed and re-check before citing in the pitch. Coverage gap: the surviving verified claims address only research angles 1 and 2 (STT and TTS models); angles 3-5 — the transport layer (Wi-Fi Direct/Wi-Fi Aware/BLE throughput, Bluetooth SPP, ESP32/LoRa bridging, Unishox2/Indic-Unicode compression ratios), the ISRO context (NavIC short-message service, GAGAN/GEMINI, Distress Alert Transmitter byte budgets, semantic-communication framing vs Lyra/EnCodec), and the competition landscape (Briar/Bridgefy/Meshtastic, past SIH approaches, Bhashini on-device efforts) — produced no verified claims and remain unresearched; the solution architecture should not treat those areas as settled. Time-sensitivity: model catalogs churn quickly — the sherpa-onnx pages contain models dated Feb 2026 and the Piper mr_IN voice landed ~1 month ago, so per-language coverage gaps (especially sherpa-onnx streaming Indic ASR and Piper gu/kn/ta/or) may close before the hackathon; Vosk WER figures are Alpha Cephei self-reported (~2021-22 challenge sets) and the Google/Azure comparison numbers are mid-2023 zero-shot measurements. License findings mix formal license files (MIT LICENSE.txt, CC-BY-NC tags — strong) with one inference (whether Indic-TTS's repo MIT formally covers the checkpoint binaries — supported by AI4Bharat's 'we open-source all models' statement but not a per-asset license grant). RTF numbers are Raspberry Pi 4 measurements used as a conservative proxy for phone SoCs, not actual Android-device measurements. One claim each in the Vosk-coverage and Indic-TTS-coverage findings passed on a 2-1 split vote; both were nonetheless verified against live primary sources with high-confidence evidence.
openQuestions: What are the real-world throughput, pairing latency, and multi-hop constraints of the candidate transport layers (Wi-Fi Direct vs Wi-Fi Aware vs Bluetooth RFCOMM/SPP vs BLE GATT with negotiated MTU) on low-end Android, and what compression ratio does Unishox2/smaz actually achieve on short Devanagari/Dravidian UTF-8 sentences — the entire angle-3 byte-budget story is unverified?

What are ISRO's concrete per-message byte/bitrate budgets for NavIC short-message service, GEMINI/GAGAN alert dissemination, and the fishermen Distress Alert Transmitter — the numbers needed to make the 'text-over-low-bitrate beats neural audio codecs' argument quantitative and the solution non-generic?

Can IndicConformer-600M (or its ~120M per-language variants) be int8-quantized/distilled to fit a sherpa-onnx or ONNX-Runtime-Mobile Android pipeline within a ~50-90 MB per-language budget, and what WER degradation does quantization cost on Kathbath/Vistaar — no verified on-device accuracy numbers exist for any quantized Indic model?

Do the sherpa-onnx tts-models release's Indic voices (Piper hi/ml, Coqui/Mimic3 bn/gu) carry SIH-eligible dataset licenses, and what is the actual on-Android RTF and RAM footprint of the ~1.5 GB Indic-TTS FastPitch checkpoints after export — i.e., which of the two license-safe TTS paths (AI4Bharat export vs Piper/community voices plus 4 custom-trained gaps) is cheaper for a hackathon timeline?
